title: Surgical Approaches to Orbital Fractures: A Practical and Systematic Review
article_subtype: Practical review comparing surgical approaches and postoperative complication rates
condition_or_topic: Surgical approaches for orbital wall fractures
clinical_background: Orbital fractures account for up to 40% of midface traumatic injuries. They may affect only the orbital walls or extend to the orbital rim, and may occur alone or within more complex fractures. Evaluation focuses on vision, eye movements, sensation, and orbital stability; orbital computed tomography is used to confirm the diagnosis. Certain findings, including a positive oculo-cardiac reflex or pediatric orbital floor entrapment, require urgent attention. Although many publications describe operative techniques, few compare outcomes across approaches, and the single randomized trial comparing open approaches did not include endoscopic surgery.
objectives: Provide an evidence-based overview of the major surgical approaches to orbital wall fractures and clarify the risks and benefits of each.
Compare postoperative complication rates across the approaches to identify which has the lowest rate.
clinical_question: In patients undergoing surgical fixation of orbital wall fractures (P), how do the subciliary, transcaruncular, transconjunctival, subtarsal, and endoscopic approaches (I/C) compare in postoperative complications (O)?
study_design: Systematic review of surgical approaches to orbital wall fractures. PubMed, including PubMed Central, MEDLINE and Bookshelf, was searched in June 2021 using combinations of “orbital,” “wall,” “fracture,” and “surgery.” PRISMA 2020 guided study identification and selection, which were performed by two independent researchers.

population.description: Patients in included studies who underwent surgery for traumatic orbital wall fractures.
inclusion_criteria: Articles describing a surgical approach in patients with orbital wall fractures after 1999.
exclusion_criteria: Studies evaluating other factors, including implant types or materials.

comparators: The five surgical approaches were compared with one another.

primary: Occurrence and rate of postoperative complications by surgical approach.

statistical_methods: Complications and noncomplications were summed for each approach and entered into a five by two cross-tabulation. A chi-square test assessed the relationship between surgical approach and complication rate using PROC FREQ with the “chisq” option in SAS version 9.4. Statistical significance was set at P value less than 0.05.
follow_up: Across the included studies, follow-up ranged from 2 weeks to 63 months.
interpretation: The review found the lowest complication rates with the subtarsal (8.2%) and transcaruncular (14.0%) approaches; higher rates were reported with the transconjunctival (36.2%), subciliary (21.4%) and endoscopic (20.2%) approaches. Among 131 patients treated through a subtarsal approach, nine (6.9%) had a scar, five (3.82%) had scleral show, three (2.29%) had ectropion, two (1.53%) had lid edema, one (0.76%) had epiphora and one (0.76%) had keratoconjunctivitis sicca. The authors observed scarring more often after subtarsal than subciliary surgery. They consider the apparent complication advantage relevant to approach selection, while acknowledging that differences among the included studies hinder direct comparison of specific complications.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors state that their findings are consistent with Bähr’s 1992 study, which reported complication rates of 8.8% for the subtarsal approach, 25% for the subciliary approach and 30.4% for the transcaruncular approach. Bähr et al also identified scarring and scleral show as frequent subtarsal complications. Heckler et al proposed that differences in muscle mobility and skin quality contribute to greater scarring with subtarsal than subciliary incisions; the authors also cite the greater distance of a subtarsal incision from the lash line as a reason a scar may be more noticeable. In contrast, Oztel et al reported no visible scar in 61 of 67 patients treated through a subtarsal incision. In a comparison cited by the authors, Han et al found no significant difference between endoscopic and transcaruncular approaches in improvement of enophthalmos, diplopia and extraocular movement limitation: the average reduction rates were 89.2% and 90.7%, respectively. Han et al reported longer operations, longer hospital stays and higher costs with the endoscopic approach.
clinical_implications: Complications associated with surgical approaches, including retrobulbar hemorrhage, infection, intraorbital hemorrhage or hematoma, and sensory injury, can potentially result in blindness, although the authors describe that outcome as unlikely.

The authors consider surgical exposure and access important when choosing an approach. They state that subtarsal and transcaruncular incisions provide more direct, wider exposure of the orbital floor than endoscopic and transconjunctival approaches.
practice_implications: The authors favor subtarsal or transcaruncular approaches at present because they describe them as low-complexity, low-cost procedures that provide direct access to the orbital floor and infraorbital rim through minimally invasive incisions.
The authors say subtarsal incisions should be considered for orbital wall reconstruction despite concern about visible scarring.
When a fracture also involves the lateral orbital border, the authors state that a subtarsal incision can be extended laterally at the canthus.
limitations: Heterogeneity among the included studies makes complications associated with different approaches difficult to compare.
The retrospective nature of the included articles and their differing follow-up periods may have affected the reported complication rates.
The authors acknowledge possible selection bias arising from efforts to make the data uniform.
open_questions: Which approach provides the fewest complications and the best overall outcomes for patients with orbital wall fractures remains to be determined definitively.
The authors suggest that improved endoscopic techniques might eventually make that approach standard care, but do not establish that it currently is.
future_directions: The authors call for high-quality randomized controlled trials providing level 1 evidence that compare the surgical approaches, include endoscopic techniques, and reduce the confounding present in this review.

secondary_results: The search retrieved 950 articles. The review included 25 manuscripts published between 1999 and 2020.
Across included studies, patient counts ranged from four to 103, with 1137 patients in total. Reported follow-up ranged from 2 weeks to 63 months.

The included studies evaluated the transcaruncular approach in six studies, the endoscopic approach in 12, the transconjunctival approach in seven, the subciliary approach in three, and the subtarsal approach in four.

In the cited Bähr study from 1992, complication rates were 8.8% for the subtarsal approach, 25% for the subciliary approach, and 30.4% for the transcaruncular approach; the authors describe the subtarsal incidence as significantly lower.
In the cited Oztel et al study from 2021, 61 of 67 patients treated through a subtarsal incision had no visible scar.

Average reduction rates were 89.2% for the endoscopic approach and 90.7% for the transcaruncular approach; operation time, hospital stay, and cost were higher with the endoscopic approach.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Orbital fractures account for a substantial share of midface injuries. This review examines the principal operations for orbital wall fractures and compares their reported complications.

document_sections.heading: Method
document_sections.content: The authors systematically reviewed postoperative complications after fixation of orbital wall fractures using subciliary, transcaruncular, transconjunctival, subtarsal, or endoscopic approaches. They searched PubMed, including PubMed Central, MEDLINE and Bookshelf, with combinations of “orbital,” “wall,” “fracture,” and “surgery.”

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The search yielded 950 articles; 25 were included, covering 1137 fractures. Endoscopic surgery was the most frequent approach (33.3%), followed by transconjunctival (32.8%), subciliary (13.5%), subtarsal (11.5%), and transcaruncular (8.9%) surgery. The transconjunctival approach had a statistically significantly higher complication rate (36.19%), followed by subciliary (21.4%) and endoscopic (20.2%, P < 0.0001) approaches. The subtarsal approach had a statistically significantly lower complication rate (8.2%), followed by the transcaruncular approach (14.0%, P < 0.0001).

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: The lowest reported complication rates occurred with subtarsal and transcaruncular surgery; rates were higher with transconjunctival, subciliary, and endoscopic surgery.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Orbital fractures represent up to 40% of midface traumatic injuries. They may be confined to orbital walls or extend to the orbital rim, and may occur alone or within more extensive injuries, including zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures, Le Fort II fractures (orbital floor fractures), and naso-orbital ethmoid fractures. Under the hydraulic theory, force applied to the globe travels backward to fracture the orbital wall. This mechanism is more likely to produce an isolated orbital floor fracture than a medial wall fracture because ethmoid air cells support the medial wall; cadaver experiments indicate that high-energy force can fracture both walls. Under the buckling theory, force applied to the orbital rim and adjacent structures travels through the wall until it reaches a weak area. The medial orbital wall is the most common fracture site (54.9%), particularly its thin lamina papyracea. Other reported patterns are combined medial wall and nasal fractures (46%), combined naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures (26.8%), isolated inferior wall fractures (18.3%), zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures (3%), and inferior orbital rim fractures (1%). Initial care should follow Advance Trauma Life Support guidance for maxillofacial injuries. History and examination should address blurred or double vision and visual loss; impaired extraocular movement, altered sensation, or orbital instability should heighten suspicion of fracture. A positive oculo-cardiac reflex requires immediate attention and treatment: its triad comprises bradycardia, nausea, and syncope, and prompt care is needed to avert fatal cardiac arrhythmia (1:3500). Orbital computed tomography is the diagnostic gold standard. In floor fractures, coronal views of the inferior and medial rectus muscles are essential for assessing possible entrapment and diplopia. Medial wall fractures are strongly associated with enophthalmos caused by collapse of the lamina papyracea or medial rectus entrapment. Computed tomography findings indicating immediate surgical correction include an orbital apex fracture with deteriorating vision, globe or optic nerve injury, periorbital emphysema, retrobulbar hematoma, and a bone fragment causing impingement. In children, the orbital floor may return to position while trapping tissue, also creating a surgical emergency. Once surgery is recommended, an approach must be selected. The described options are subciliary, subtarsal, transcaruncular/transconjunctival, and endoscopic surgery. Most publications emphasize technique rather than comparative outcomes, and only one randomized control trial compared open approaches without assessing endoscopy. The review aims to clarify each approach’s risks and benefits and identify the lowest-complication option.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: This systematic review compared postoperative complications among subciliary, transcaruncular, transconjunctival, subtarsal, and endoscopic approaches to orbital wall fractures. A supplementary table details complications by included study. In June 2021, the authors searched PubMed, including PubMed Central, MEDLINE and Bookshelf, using combinations of “orbital,” “wall,” “fracture,” and “surgery.” They applied PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidance to identify and select articles. Two independent researchers, M.P. and J.J., gathered preliminary information and selected manuscripts against the eligibility criteria. Eligible articles described an operative approach for patients with orbital wall fractures after 1999. Earlier studies were omitted because approaches had evolved and most did not report complications separately by approach. Studies of implant or material types, novel approaches, nontraumatic operations, and nonEnglish articles were also excluded.

document_sections.heading: Takeaways
document_sections.content: The review asks how the approaches to orbital wall fractures differ in risks and benefits and which has the lowest complication rate. Its findings identify statistically significantly lower complication rates with subtarsal and transcaruncular surgery. The authors emphasize understanding each method’s risks when selecting an approach.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: The authors summed complications and noncomplications separately for each of five approaches. They constructed a five by two table crossing endoscopic, subciliary, subtarsal, transcaruncular, and transconjunctival surgery with complication status (yes/no). A chi-square test assessed the association between approach and complication rate, using PROC FREQ with the “chisq” option in SAS version 9.4. Statistical significance was defined as a P value less than 0.05.

document_sections.heading: Subciliary
document_sections.content: Converse introduced this approach in 1944 for orbital floor fractures. Its usual skin incision follows a crease several millimeters below and parallel to the eyelashes, extending from the medial punctum to 15mm beyond the lateral canthus. Dissection separates skin from orbicularis beneath the tarsal plate, then passes through orbicularis fibers toward the orbital septum and infraorbital rim; the periosteum is opened to reach the fracture. Staggering the dissection planes aims to prevent direct eyelid scarring and scar inversion. In the subciliary skin-flap variation, orbicularis fibers are divided at the level of the periosteal incision rather than beneath the tarsus. In the nonstepped skin-muscle variation, skin and orbicularis are incised together to the tarsal plate before dissection follows the preseptal plane. Compared with a skin-only flap, the skin-muscle approach appears to offer better aesthetic results, less skin necrosis and ecchymosis, and less ectropion. The subciliary approach has nevertheless been associated with more denervation of the pretarsal orbicularis.

document_sections.heading: Subtarsal
document_sections.content: Converse also developed the subtarsal approach. The incision follows the lower edge of the tarsal plate within the subtarsal fold. With edema, it is placed 5–7mm from the lower eyelid margin along an inferolateral course approximating the usual fold. Orbicularis is divided in the direction of its fibers beneath the skin incision, and preseptal dissection proceeds to the infraorbital rim. This technique aims to avoid scar inversion while retaining all pretarsal and much preseptal orbicularis innervation.

document_sections.heading: Transcaruncular/Transconjunctival
document_sections.content: Transconjunctival access to the infraorbital rim may follow a retroseptal or preseptal route. The retroseptal route passes from a conjunctival incision directly into lower-eyelid fat compartments and then to the rim. The preseptal route starts just below the tarsal border, enters the suborbicularis oculi/preseptal space above the junction of the lower lid retractors and orbital septum, and reaches the rim through a supraperiosteal plane. For medial wall access, a medial conjunctival incision is made along the semilunar fold behind the lacrimal drainage system; it may be precaruncular or transcaruncular. Dissection continues within periorbital soft tissue to the posterior lacrimal crest. The lacrimal system remains intact, and an incision through periorbital tissue exposes the medial wall.

document_sections.heading: Endoscopic
document_sections.content: Endoscopic techniques have developed since the 1990s and are generally transnasal. Earlier procedures included medial infundibulectomy with a sickle knife, removal of the uncinate process with forceps by subluxation, and widening of the maxillary ostium to permit fracture identification with a 30-degree or 70-degree endoscope. A ureteral balloon catheter could elevate displaced orbital contents; balloon support was used because those procedures lacked rigid fixation. Contemporary access is also usually transnasal, although transconjunctival access is possible. Standard instruments include 4-mm rigid nasal endoscopes (0degree and 30degrees). Wide maxillary antrostomy provides floor access, while anterior ethmoidectomy permits assessment of the medial wall relative to the floor. The described technique creates an isolated orbital floor fracture with herniation of orbital contents, removes unstable fragments, and places a porous polyethylene plate (MEDPOR; Stryker Corporation) within the defect. Balloon use in the maxillary sinus to reduce orbital fat causes more discomfort than nasal packing, which is now preferred. Potential complications include discomfort, injury to nearby structures, and increased infection, particularly with packing compared with balloon inflation. Advantages include improved anatomical visualization and aesthetic results. Otolaryngologists generally use this approach, whose validity has been accepted in many studies.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The search retrieved 950 articles. After eligibility assessment, 25 manuscripts published between 1999 and 2020 were included. Individual studies enrolled from four to 103 patients, totaling 1137 patients. Six studies assessed transcaruncular surgery; 12, endoscopic surgery; seven, transconjunctival surgery; three, subciliary surgery; and four, subtarsal surgery. Reported follow-up ranged from 2 weeks to 63 months. Table 1 presents the included studies, their approaches, complications, and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: COMPARISON BETWEEN SURGICAL APPROACHES
document_sections.content: The analysis covered 1137 orbital fractures. Endoscopic surgery was most frequent (33.3%); among external approaches, transconjunctival surgery accounted for 32.8%, subciliary for 13.5%, subtarsal for 11.5%, and transcaruncular for 8.9%. The overall complication incidence across approaches was 22.6%. Reported complications comprised diplopia, motor deficit, ptosis, entropion, ectropion, enophthalmos, corneal injury, proptosis, lagophthalmos, keratoconjuntivitis sicca, visual disturbance, scarring, epiphora, scleral show, asymmetry, intraorbital hemorrhage, trichiasis, implant misplacement, canthal dystopia, hyperpigmentation, lower-eyelid skin dimpling, lid edema, infection, and blepharoptosis. By approach, the statistically significantly higher complication rate occurred with transconjunctival surgery (36.2%), followed by subciliary (21.4%) and endoscopic surgery (20.2%, P < 0.0001). Subtarsal surgery had the statistically significantly lowest rate (8.2%), followed by transcaruncular surgery (14.0%, P < 0.0001). Table 2 compares complications and their absence across approaches.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The authors review initial fracture assessment and operative access. They stress documenting approach-associated retrobulbar hemorrhage, infection, intraorbital hemorrhage or hematoma, and sensory injury because these complications could cause blindness, although that outcome is unlikely. Their analysis found the lowest complication rates with subtarsal and transcaruncular approaches. Earlier transcutaneous reconstruction raised concern about visible scars, particularly in comparison with conjunctival or endoscopic methods. The authors relate their findings to Bähr’s 1992 study, which reported significantly fewer complications with subtarsal surgery (8.8%) than with subciliary (25%) or transcaruncular surgery (30.4%). In the present review, the subtarsal rate was 8.2%. Among 131 subtarsal patients, nine (6.9%) had a scar, five (3.82%) had scleral show, three (2.29%) had ectropion, two (1.53%) had lid edema, one (0.76%) had epiphora, and one (0.76%) had keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Bähr et al likewise identified scarring and scleral show as the most frequent subtarsal complications. The authors observed scarring more often after subtarsal than subciliary surgery. Heckler et al proposed poorer muscle mobility and skin quality at the subtarsal site as an explanation; placing the incision farther from the eyelashes may also make a scar more noticeable. In contrast, Oztel et al reported in 2021 that 61 of 67 subtarsal patients had no visible scar. Although conjunctival incisions do not produce a visible scar, the authors interpret those findings as suggesting that subtarsal scarring may be limited and that subtarsal access should be considered for orbital wall reconstruction. Operative exposure must also inform approach selection. The authors describe transcaruncular and subtarsal incisions as providing broader direct floor exposure than endoscopic and transconjunctival approaches; a subtarsal incision can be extended laterally at the canthus when the lateral orbital border is also fractured. Endoscopy has been pursued for less invasive access and aesthetic results comparable to transcutaneous methods. In a comparison by Han et al, improvement in enophthalmos, diplopia, and restricted extraocular movement did not differ significantly between endoscopic endonasal reduction and transcaruncular surgery; average reduction rates were 89.2% and 90.7%, respectively. Han et al also found longer operations and hospital stays and higher costs with endoscopy. The authors suggest that improved endoscopic techniques may eventually become standard care, but currently prefer subtarsal or transcaruncular procedures because of their low complexity and cost. Both use minimally invasive incisions and directly access the orbital floor and infraorbital rim.

document_sections.heading: LIMITATIONS
document_sections.content: Heterogeneity among the included studies is the principal limitation and hinders comparison of complication types between approaches. The retrospective nature of the included articles and differences in follow-up could have affected complication rates. The authors also acknowledge possible selection bias while attempting to make the data uniform. They call for level 1 evidence comparing these approaches, including endoscopic techniques; high-quality randomized controlled trials could lessen confounding and establish which approach yields the fewest complications and best overall outcomes. Despite these limitations, the authors believe their review helps identify the approach with the lowest complication rate for orbital wall reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: Subtarsal and transcaruncular approaches had the lowest observed complication rates, while transconjunctival, subciliary, and endoscopic approaches had higher reported rates. Further research is needed to determine the best approach for patients with orbital wall fractures.

tables.summary: Among the approaches compared, the subtarsal group had the smallest share of reported complications and the transconjunctival group the largest. The table reports a statistically significant relationship between approach and complication occurrence by chi-square test (P < 0.0001).

main_conclusion: The authors observed the lowest complication rates with subtarsal and transcaruncular access, while rates were higher with transconjunctival, subciliary, and endoscopic access. They state that further research is needed to establish the best approach for orbital wall fractures.
narrative_summary: This systematic review compared postoperative complications after surgical approaches to orbital wall fractures. A PubMed search yielded 950 articles; 25 studies published between 1999 and 2020 were included, covering 1137 fractures. The approaches assessed were endoscopic, transconjunctival, subciliary, subtarsal, and transcaruncular. Across approaches, the reported complication incidence was 22.6%. In the comparison table, complication counts were 21 (8.2%) for subtarsal access, 36 (14.0%) for transcaruncular access, 52 (20.2%) for endoscopic access, 55 (21.4%) for subciliary access, and 93 (36.2%) for transconjunctival access. The association between surgical approach and complication occurrence was statistically significant (P < 0.0001). Reported problems included diplopia, eyelid malposition, enophthalmos, scarring, visual disturbances, hemorrhage, and infection. The authors favor considering subtarsal and transcaruncular approaches because they observed fewer complications and describe these procedures as relatively low in complexity and cost, with direct exposure. They caution that heterogeneity among studies, their retrospective nature, differences in follow-up, and possible selection bias limit comparisons. They call for high-quality randomized trials that include endoscopic techniques before the approach with the best overall outcomes can be determined definitively.
